common_name: Southern Annual Saltmarsh Aster / Slim Aster (Blackweed)
field_group: Annual, narrow-leaved, small-headed open-branching aster of disturbed ground and open habitats
project_tracker_diagnostic: Annual or short-lived taprooted, usually nearly glabrous slim/wiry herb; leaves narrow linear to lanceolate-linear (often 1–3.5 mm wide), many small lilac/pinkish-rayed heads in a highly diffuse array with conspicuous space between heads. NOT Eurybia divaricata (white wood aster).

project_inclusion.learning_reason: Common or useful Central Texas fall/white composite for field learning.

morphology_keys.life_cycle: Annual to short-lived perennial, taprooted, not a persistent clump-forming woodland perennial (UT Williamson County flora).
morphology_keys.habit: Wiry, loosely branched, very airy/open paniculate herb, usually <60 cm in local range; may be dwarfed in lawns and disturbed ground.
morphology_keys.leaves: Helically alternate, simple, sessile or nearly so, narrow linear to oblanceolate-linear/lanceolate-linear, mostly 10–60 × 1–3.5 mm; margins entire to minutely toothed; not broad triangular, cordate, or long-petiolate woodland leaves.
morphology_keys.heads: Small radiate heads ~8–20 mm across, roughly 14–21 ray florets, 18–50 disc florets, pale pinkish/lilac to white-lavender; heads widely spaced and apparently floating on fine peduncles.
morphology_keys.phyllaries: 20–25 phyllaries in 3–5 series, unequal, narrow outer ones with conspicuously membranous margins; inspect scaled side view, especially against true S. subulatum.
morphology_keys.stem: Nearly glabrous stems grooved below leaves; short hairs occasionally on lower internodes.
morphology_keys.fruit: Narrow cypselae with pale capillary pappus bristles; fruit details secondary to habit/leaf/head architecture.
best_field_traits: NARROW linear to linear-lanceolate mostly sessile leaves, only ~1–3.5 mm wide.
Very open, widely spaced inflorescence heads; large gaps between heads.
Taprooted ANNUAL to short-lived herb with slim ±glabrous grooved stems.
Small (8–20 mm) pink-lilac to pale ray heads.
S. subulatum = denser pyramidal flowering array, more southeastern coastal/saline; habitat alone cannot prove the split.
Do not confuse with Eurybia divaricata (white wood aster): perennial shade plant with broad, heart-shaped/petiolate serrate leaves.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: S. divaricatum (formerly treated under S. subulatum var. ligulatum) is the widespread inland Texas southern annual saltmarsh aster. True S. subulatum has a relatively dense pyramidal flowering array and limited southeast saline Texas distribution. Eurybia divaricata, WHITE WOOD ASTER, is a different genus and life-history concept.

look_here_first: Check the skinny alternate, mostly sessile leaves (often 1–3.5 mm wide), nearly hairless wiry stems, and VERY OPEN diffuse head arrangement. This Texas saltmarsh-aster complex taxon is usually annual or short-lived and taprooted—not the perennial shade-loving white wood aster Eurybia divaricata. Compare with true S. subulatum: that taxon tends to have a denser pyramidal flowering array and primarily southeastern saline/coastal Texas distribution.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Against S. subulatum, check open, diffuse flower spacing vs more dense pyramidal array, scaled phyllary form, and inland Texas versus southeastern saline/coastal context. Against Eurybia divaricata, narrow alternate nearly sessile leaves and annual taprooted habit vs broad triangular-cordate petiolate leaves and perennial woodland habit.

taxonomic_note: IMPORTANT historical learner correction 2026-10-12: this record was erroneously labeled 'White Woodland Aster' and described as a broad-serrate-leaved shade perennial (characteristics of Eurybia divaricata, a different genus). Corrected to the accepted southern annual saltmarsh aster/slim aster concept Symphyotrichum divaricatum. FNA/ITIS may place this concept under S. subulatum var. ligulatum; existing project rule retains S. divaricatum separate from true S. subulatum, following the newer Texas treatment. Taxon photographs already pulled from exact S. divaricatum iNaturalist taxon 169457; individual observation identifications are NOT independently reverified here.
